claim: Sulfolobus acidocaldarius is a hyperthermophilic and acidophilic Crenarchaeon that thrives in acidic thermal soils and hot springs worldwide.
source: Sulfolobus acidocaldarius is a hyperthermophilic and acidophilic Crenarchaeon and thrives in acidic thermal soils and hot springs worldwide.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the manuscript describing the organism's characteristics and habitat.

claim: Sulfolobus acidocaldarius grows at pH ~2–3 and temperatures ranging from 65 to 90°C.
source: It grows at pH ~2–3 and temperatures ranging from 65 to 90°C (Brock et al., 1972).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brock et al., 1972.

claim: The Sulfolobus S-layer is composed of two repeating glycoproteins, SlaA and SlaB.
source: The Sulfolobus S-layer is composed of two repeating glycoproteins, SlaA and SlaB.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the composition of the S-layer.

claim: In S. acidocaldarius, SlaA contains 1424 amino acids and has a molecular mass of 151 kDa.
source: In S. acidocaldarius, SlaA contains 1424 amino acids and has a molecular mass of 151 kDa, whereas SlaB comprises 475 amino acids and has a mass of 49.5 kDa (Grogan, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grogan, 1996.

claim: SlaB comprises 475 amino acids and has a mass of 49.5 kDa.
source: In S. acidocaldarius, SlaA contains 1424 amino acids and has a molecular mass of 151 kDa, whereas SlaB comprises 475 amino acids and has a mass of 49.5 kDa (Grogan, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grogan, 1996.

claim: SlaA is predicted to be a soluble protein rich in β-strands.
source: Comparative sequence analysis and molecular modelling predicted that SlaA is a soluble protein rich in β-strands (Veith et al., 2009).
evidence: This prediction is supported by a citation to Veith et al., 2009.

claim: SlaB is predicted to contain three consecutive β-sandwich domains at the N-terminus and a membrane-bound coiled-coil domain at the C-terminus.
source: On the other hand, SlaB has been predicted to contain three consecutive β-sandwich domains at the N-terminus and a membrane-bound coiled-coil domain at the C-terminus (Veith et al., 2009).
evidence: This prediction is supported by a citation to Veith et al., 2009.

claim: Across the Sulfolobales, SlaA shows higher sequence and structural variability compared to SlaB.
source: Across the Sulfolobales, SlaA shows higher sequence and structural variability compared to SlaB (Veith et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Veith et al., 2009.

claim: The S. acidocaldarius S-layer was described as a 'smooth', highly porous, hexagonal (p3) lattice by early 2D crystallography and electron microscopy experiments.
source: Early 2D crystallography and electron microscopy experiments described the S. acidocaldarius S-layer as a 'smooth', highly porous, hexagonal (p3) lattice (Grogan, 1996; Taylor et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grogan, 1996 and Taylor et al., 1982.

claim: The S. acidocaldarius S-layer has a bipartite organisation with SlaA and SlaB forming the extracellular- and intracellular-facing layers, respectively.
source: The S-layer has a bipartite organisation with SlaA and SlaB forming the extracellular- and intracellular-facing layers, respectively.
evidence: This statement is based on previous work by the authors as cited (Gambelli et al., 2019).

claim: Dimers of SlaA and trimers of SlaB assemble around hexagonal and triangular pores, creating a ~30-nm-thick canopy-like framework.
source: Dimers of SlaA and trimers of SlaB assemble around hexagonal and triangular pores, creating a ~30-nm-thick canopy-like framework.
evidence: This statement is based on previous work by the authors as cited (Gambelli et al., 2019).

claim: Sulfolobus mutants lacking SlaA and/or SlaB show morphological aberrations, higher sensitivity to hyperosmotic stress and alterations of the chromosome copy number.
source: Sulfolobus mutants lacking SlaA and/or SlaB show morphological aberrations, higher sensitivity to hyperosmotic stress and alterations of the chromosome copy number, suggesting that in these species the S-layer plays key roles in cell integrity, maintenance, and cell division (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: The structure of SlaA30–1069 was determined at 3.1 Å global resolution using single-particle cryo electron microscopy.
source: The final cryoEM map had a global resolution of 3.1 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a, b and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by figures showing the resolution.

claim: Residues 30–1069 (~70% of the sequence) of SlaA were clearly defined in the cryoEM map.
source: Residues 30–1069 (~70% of the sequence) were clearly defined in the cryoEM map.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the portion of the protein resolved in the structure.

claim: The N-terminal signal peptide (predicted to be residues 1–24) of SlaA is cleaved prior to S-layer assembly.
source: The N-terminal signal peptide (predicted to be residues 1–24) is cleaved prior to S-layer assembly (Veith et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Veith et al., 2009.

claim: Residues 1070–1424 at the C-terminus of SlaA were not resolved by single-particle analysis, likely due to their high flexibility.
source: A few N-terminal residues and residues 1070–1424 at the C-terminus were not resolved by SPA, likely due to their high flexibility (Figure 1—figure supplement 5a; Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and videos showing flexibility.

claim: SlaA30–1069 is a Y-shaped protein consisting mostly of β-strands and containing only a few short α-helices.
source: SlaA30–1069 is a Y-shaped protein. It consists mostly of β-strands and contains only a few short α-helices (Figure 1a, b, Figure 1—figure supplement 4c, d).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by structural figures.

claim: The polypeptide chain of SlaA30–1069 is arranged into four domains (D1, D2, D3, and D4).
source: The polypeptide chain is arranged into four domains (D130–234, D2235–660,701–746, D3661–700,747–914, and D4915–1069), as defined by SWORD (Postic et al., 2017; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to domain assignment software and supported by figures.

claim: Only domain D4 of SlaA shows significant similarity to known structures, specifically domain 3 of complement C5.
source: Of those domains, only D4 shows significant similarity to known structures – the domain 3 of complement C5 (PDB ID: 4E0S) according to DALI (Holm, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by structural comparison using DALI and a citation.

claim: A disulphide bond links domains D3 and D4 of SlaA (Cys677–Cys1017).
source: A disulphide bond links D3 and D4 (Cys677–Cys1017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4d), however, the density of this bond is not visible in the cryoEM map, likely due to electron beam damage (Kato et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to a figure and a citation explaining why it's not visible.

claim: The structure of the missing C-terminus (SlaA914–1424) was predicted using Alphafold and revealed two additional β-domains, D5 and D6.
source: The structure of the missing C-terminus (SlaA914–1424) was predicted (including D4 to aid alignment) using Alphafold (Jumper et al., 2021) and revealed two additional β-domains, D5 and D6 (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Alphafold and supporting figures.

claim: Alphafold predicted five different conformations of SlaA914–1424, which differed with regard to the position of D5–D6 relative to D1–D4, suggesting an in-plane flexibility between these two parts of the protein around a hinge.
source: Alphafold predicted five different conformations of SlaA914–1424, which differed with regard to the position of D5–D6 relative to D1–D4, suggesting an in-plane flexibility between these two parts of the protein around a hinge (amino acids A1067–L1071) between D4 and D5 (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Alphafold predictions and supporting figures.

claim: The hinge between D4 and D5 of SlaA is located at amino acids A1067–L1071.
source: Alphafold predicted five different conformations of SlaA914–1424, which differed with regard to the position of D5–D6 relative to D1–D4, suggesting an in-plane flexibility between these two parts of the protein around a hinge (amino acids A1067–L1071) between D4 and D5 (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Alphafold predictions.

claim: Similar conformations to those predicted by Alphafold were observed in 2D classes of the cryoEM dataset and a low-resolution 3D refinement of SlaA purified from Saccharolobus solfataricus.
source: Similar conformations were also observed in 2D classes of our cryoEM dataset (Figure 1—figure supplement 5a, Video 2), as well as a low-resolution 3D refinement of SlaA purified from the related species Saccharolobus solfataricus (Figure 1—figure supplement 5b, c), substantiating the Alphafold predictions in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to supporting figures and videos.

claim: The jackknife-like flexibility of SlaA aids its assembly into an interwoven S-layer.
source: It is probable that this jackknife-like flexibility aids SlaA's assembly into an interwoven S-layer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed flexibility.

claim: If flexibility is retained in the assembled S-layer, it will enable the S-layer to adopt various degrees of curvature, necessitated by its ability to encapsulate large cells and small exosomes.
source: If some of this flexibility is retained in the assembled S-layer, it will enable it to adopt various degrees of curvature, necessitated by its ability to encapsulate large cells, as well as small exosomes.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed flexibility.

claim: SlaA is expected to be highly glycosylated with 31 predicted N-glycosylation sites.
source: SlaA is expected to be highly glycosylated; its sequence contains 31 predicted N-glycosylation sites (Peyfoon et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Peyfoon et al., 2010.

claim: The cryoEM map of SlaA30–1069 shows 19 glycan densities.
source: Our cryoEM map of SlaA30–1069 shows 19 glycan densities (Figure 2), largely in agreement with the prediction of 20 sequons located in this portion of the protein (Peyfoon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing glycan densities.

claim: The entire SlaA protein contains a total of 27 confirmed glycans.
source: Therefore, the entire SlaA protein contains a total of 27 confirmed glycans.
evidence: This is stated based on the combination of cryoEM data and mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Eight glycosylation sites in domains D5 and D6 of SlaA were confirmed by mass spectrometry analysis.
source: The remaining predicted glycosylation sites reside in domains D5 and D6, in which eight sites were confirmed to be glycosylated by mass spectrometry analysis (Peyfoon et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Peyfoon et al., 2010.

claim: The N-glycans were modelled into the cryoEM densities based on their known chemical structure.
source: The N-glycans were modelled into the cryoEM densities based on their known chemical structure (Zähringer et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zähringer et al., 2000.

claim: The complete glycan is a tribranched hexasaccharide, containing a 6-sulfoquinovose (QuiS).
source: The complete glycan is a tribranched hexasaccharide, containing a 6-sulfoquinovose (QuiS).
evidence: This is stated based on known chemical structure.

claim: Most glycans (47%) were built as pentasaccharides, lacking the glucose bound to QuiS in the mature glycan.
source: Most glycans (47 %) were built as pentasaccharides, lacking the glucose bound to QuiS in the mature glycan; 15% of the glycan pool could be modelled with the whole hexasaccharide structure.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryoEM data.

claim: 15% of the glycan pool could be modelled with the whole hexasaccharide structure.
source: Most glycans (47 %) were built as pentasaccharides, lacking the glucose bound to QuiS in the mature glycan; 15% of the glycan pool could be modelled with the whole hexasaccharide structure.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryoEM data.

claim: Glycan volume occupancy was comparable on the open and closed conformations of SlaA monomers.
source: Glycan volume occupancy was comparable on the two conformations of the monomers (Figure 2g, h).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing GlycoSHIELD models.

claim: Both closed and open conformations of SlaA showed a similar number of possible glycan conformers, signifying that neither conformation is entropically favoured over the other.
source: Both closed and open conformations showed a similar number of possible glycan conformers (with the closed slightly more than the open form; Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This signifies that neither SlaA conformation is entropically favoured over the other, which allows for the observed free jackknife movement between D1–4 and D5–6 (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing glycan conformer analysis.

claim: SlaA assembly and disassembly are pH-sensitive processes.
source: SlaA assembly and disassembly are pH-sensitive processes (Gambelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gambelli et al., 2019.

claim: A pH shift from acidic (~pH 4) to alkaline (~pH 10) induces the disassembly of the S-layer lattice into its component subunits.
source: A pH shift from acidic (~pH 4) to alkaline (~pH 10) induces the disassembly of the lattice into its component subunits, while a reassembly occurs upon shifting the pH back to acidic (Gambelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gambelli et al., 2019.

claim: Reassembly of the S-layer occurs upon shifting the pH back to acidic.
source: A pH shift from acidic (~pH 4) to alkaline (~pH 10) induces the disassembly of the lattice into its component subunits, while a reassembly occurs upon shifting the pH back to acidic (Gambelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gambelli et al., 2019.

claim: The cryoEM maps of SlaA30–1069 at pH 4, 7, and 10 were virtually identical, demonstrating a remarkable pH stability of this protein.
source: Strikingly, the cryoEM maps of SlaA30–1069 at the three pH conditions were virtually identical, demonstrating a remarkable pH stability of this protein.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of cryoEM maps at different pH values.

claim: The mean r.m.s.d. value of Cα atoms between the pH 4 and 10 structures of SlaA30–1069 was 0.79 Å.
source: The mean r.m.s.d. (root-mean-square deviation) value of C⍺ atoms between the pH 4 and 10 structures was 0.79 Å (min. = 0.02 Å; max. = 2.6 Å) (Figure 3b; Video 3), confirming that SlaA30–1069 maintains its structure unchanged across a surprisingly broad pH range.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing structural alignment.

claim: A pH-induced conformational change or unfolding in SlaA30–1069 is not the cause for S-layer disassembly.
source: This suggests that a pH-induced conformational change or unfolding in SlaA30–1069 is not the cause for S-layer disassembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural stability observed across pH values.

claim: The overall protein charge of SlaA changes from positive at pH 4 to negative at pH 10.
source: An analysis of the surface charges of SlaA, including the glycans, at pH 4, 7, and 10 revealed that the overall protein charge changes from positive at pH 4 to negative at pH 10 (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing electrostatic surface potential.

claim: The glycans contribute considerably to the negative charge of SlaA at higher pH values.
source: A comparison of the surface charge between glycosylated and non-glycosylated SlaA (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showed that the glycans contribute considerably to the negative charge of the protein at higher pH values.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures comparing glycosylated and non-glycosylated protein.

claim: The change in electrostatic surface potential may be a key factor in disrupting protein–protein interactions within the S-layer, causing its disassembly at alkaline pH.
source: This change in electrostatic surface potential may be a key factor in disrupting protein–protein interactions within the S-layer, causing its disassembly at alkaline pH.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed changes in surface charge.

claim: A cryoEM map of the S. acidocaldarius S-layer on exosomes was obtained at 11.2 Å resolution using subtomogram averaging.
source: To analyse the in situ structure of the S-layer, we performed STA using Warp (Tegunov and Cramer, 2019), Relion 3.1 (Scheres, 2020), and M (Tegunov et al., 2021) and obtained a cryoEM map at 11.2 Å resolution (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the subtomogram average.

claim: Six SlaA monomers assemble around a hexagonal pore of 48 Å in diameter (glycans not included).
source: Six SlaA monomers assemble around a hexagonal pore of 48 Å in diameter (glycans not included) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the assembled structure.

claim: The triangular pores in the S-layer have a diameter of ~85 Å.
source: The triangular pores that surround the hexagonal pores have a diameter of ~85 Å and are defined by the D2, D4, D5, and D6 domains of three SlaA molecules (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the assembled structure.

claim: Two SlaA monomers dimerise through the D6 domains, with each SlaA dimer spanning two adjacent hexagonal pores.
source: Two SlaA monomers dimerise through the D6 domains, with each SlaA dimer spanning two adjacent hexagonal pores (Figure 4b, d, e, Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the assembled structure.

claim: The SlaA dimer includes an angle of 160° between the two monomers, and has a total length of 420 Å.
source: The SlaA dimer includes an angle of 160° between the two monomers, and has a total length of 420 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the dimer structure.

claim: Glycans fill large gaps seen between SlaA's globular domains and significantly protrude into the lumen of the triangular and hexagonal pores.
source: Modelling of glycan shields in the assembled structure showed that glycans fill large gaps seen between SlaA's globular domains and significantly protrude into the lumen of the triangular and hexagonal pores (Figure 4f–h).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing GlycoSHIELD models.

claim: In the assembled S-layer, the interaction sites between SlaA largely occur via unglycosylated surfaces, leaving most glycans unaffected.
source: In the assembled S-layer, the interaction sites between SlaA largely occur via unglycosylated surfaces, leaving most glycans unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing glycan conformer analysis.

claim: Reduction of glycan conformational freedom is overall small between isolated and assembled SlaA monomers.
source: Reduction of glycan conformational freedom is overall small between isolated and assembled SlaA monomers.
evidence: This is stated based on glycan conformer analysis.

claim: The glycoshields appear to delineate protein–protein interfaces, which may 'guide' the self-assembly of the S-layer.
source: Instead, the glycoshields appear to delineate protein–protein interfaces, which may 'guide' the self-assembly of the S-layer, substantiated by the fact that any restriction of glycan flexibility would be entropically unfavourable.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed glycan distribution.

claim: A glycan-guided assembly mechanism has been suggested for the assembly of cadherins in the desmosome.
source: Similarly, a glycan-guided assembly mechanism has been suggested for the assembly of cadherins in the desmosome (Sikora et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sikora et al., 2020.

claim: The predicted structure for one SlaB monomer consists of three N-terminal β-sandwich domains and a 132 amino acid long C-terminal α-helix.
source: The predicted structure for one SlaB monomer consists of three N-terminal β-sandwich domains and a 132 amino acid long C-terminal α-helix (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing Alphafold predictions.

claim: Three SlaB molecules form a trimeric coiled-coil via their C-terminal α-helices, and their N-terminal β-domains fanning out into a propeller-like structure.
source: Alphafold v2.2.0 (Jumper et al., 2021) suggests that three SlaB molecules form a trimeric coiled-coil via their C-terminal ⍺-helices, and their N-terminal β-domains fanning out into a propeller-like structure (Figure 5a, b; Figure 5-figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing Alphafold predictions.

claim: The C-terminal amino acids 448–470 of SlaB are predicted as transmembrane helix by TMHMM-2.0 server.
source: The TMHMM-2.0 server predicted the C-terminal amino acids 448–470 as transmembrane helix.
evidence: This is stated based on prediction using TMHMM-2.0 server.

claim: SlaB is predicted to have 14 N-glycosylation sites, of which six are located along the C-terminal α-helix.
source: The protein is predicted to have 14 N-glycosylation sites, of which six are located along the C-terminal α-helix (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b–d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing predicted glycosylation sites.

claim: The C-terminal α-helix of SlaB is mostly neutral in electrostatic surface potential at pH 4.
source: The electrostatic surface potential calculated at pH 4 shows that the C-terminal α-helix is mostly neutral (Figure 5—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing electrostatic surface potential.

claim: The three β-sandwich domains of SlaB have greater electrostatic potential, with D2 being mostly positive and D3 carrying distinct negatively charged patches.
source: In contrast, the three β-sandwich domains have greater electrostatic potential. While D2 is mostly positive, D3 carries distinct negatively charged patches (Figure 5—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing electrostatic surface potential.

claim: The negatively charged patches in SlaB's D3 domain may play a role in electrostatic interactions between SlaB and the mainly positively charged SlaA.
source: These patches may play a role in electrostatic interactions between SlaB's D3 domain and the mainly positively charged SlaA.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed electrostatic properties.

claim: In the assembled lattice, SlaB trimers occupy alternating triangular pores around each hexagonal pore.
source: In the assembled lattice, SlaB trimers occupy alternating triangular pores around each hexagonal pore (Gambelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gambelli et al., 2019.

claim: The S-layer lattice is a ~35-nm-thick macromolecular assembly, in which each SlaB trimer interacts with three SlaA dimers.
source: The lattice is a ~35-nm-thick macromolecular assembly, in which each SlaB trimer interacts with three SlaA dimers.
evidence: This is stated based on the assembled structure.

claim: The interaction between SlaB and SlaA may be mediated by the positively charged D6 dimerising domains of SlaA and the negatively charged N-terminal Ig-like D3 domains of SlaB.
source: This interaction may be mediated by the positively charged D6 dimerising domains of SlaA and the negatively charged N-terminal Ig-like D3 domains of SlaB.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed electrostatic properties.

claim: The new data confirm the overall p3 S-layer lattice symmetry, in which the unit cell contains one SlaB trimer and three SlaA dimers (SlaB3/3SlaA2).
source: The new data confirm the overall p3 S-layer lattice symmetry, in which the unit cell contains one SlaB trimer and three SlaA dimers (SlaB3/3SlaA2).
evidence: This is stated based on the assembled structure.

claim: Each SlaB trimer occupies alternating triangular pores and each SlaA dimer spans two adjacent hexagonal pores.
source: Each SlaB trimer occupies alternating triangular pores and each SlaA dimer spans two adjacent hexagonal pores.
evidence: This is stated based on the assembled structure.

claim: SlaB trimer occupancy of all triangular pores would likely be unfavourable due to steric hindrance.
source: Because each SlaB monomer interacts with the dimerisation domains of SlaA dimers, the SlaB trimer occupancy of all triangular pores would likely be unfavourable due to steric hindrance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed structure.

claim: Alternating SlaB throughout the array would reduce the protein synthesis costs for this protein by 50%.
source: Additionally, alternating SlaB throughout the array would reduce the protein synthesis costs for this protein by 50%.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structure.

claim: SlaB trimers occupying every second triangular pore effectively create an S-layer with a variety of pore sizes, modulating the exchange of molecules with the environment.
source: SlaB trimers occupying every second triangular pore also effectively create an S-layer with a variety of pore sizes, modulating the exchange of molecules with the environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structure.

claim: The SlaA dimer spans an angle of 160° and extends over 42 nm in the revised model.
source: Here, the SlaA dimer (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a) spans an angle of 160° and extends over 42 nm, instead of 23 nm, as previously proposed (Gambelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures showing the dimer structure.

claim: The increased length of the SlaA dimer is largely a result of the unexpected positioning of domains D5 and D6.
source: The increased length is largely a result of the unexpected positioning of domains D5 and D6, which were previously not accounted for (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: SLPs of extremophilic archaea generally show a high degree of glycosylation, potentially aiding their survival in extreme environments.
source: SLPs of extremophilic archaea generally show a high degree of glycosylation, potentially aiding their survival in extreme environments (Jarrell et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jarrell et al., 2014.

claim: The presence of a heterogeneous family of glycans has been shown in the SLP of H. volcanii and the archaellum of Methanothermococcus thermolithotrophicus.
source: The presence of a heterogeneous family of glycans has also been shown, for example, in the SLP of H. volcanii (Abu-Qarn et al., 2007) and the archaellum of Methanothermococcus thermolithotrophicus (Kelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Abu-Qarn et al., 2007 and Kelly et al., 2020.

claim: In archaea, the final step in protein glycosylation is catalysed by the oligosaccharyl transferase AglB.
source: In archaea, the final step in protein glycosylation is catalysed by the oligosaccharyl transferase AglB (Meyer and Albers, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Meyer and Albers, 2014.

claim: AglB is promiscuous, meaning that AglB can load glycans of variable length on the lipid carrier.
source: The enzyme is promiscuous, meaning that AglB can load glycans of variable length on the lipid carrier (Cohen-Rosenzweig et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cohen-Rosenzweig et al., 2014.

claim: AglB is essential for the viability of S. acidocaldarius.
source: While AglB is essential for the viability of S. acidocaldarius (Meyer and Albers, 2014), it remains to be determined whether the heterogenous composition of its glycans is to be attributed to AglB loading glycan precursors onto SlaA and/or glycan hydrolysis due to the harsh environmental conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Meyer and Albers, 2014.

claim: Metal ions are often bound to SLPs and have been demonstrated to play a crucial role in S-layer assembly and cell-surface binding.
source: Metal ions are often bound to SLPs and have recently been demonstrated to play a crucial role in S-layer assembly and cell-surface binding (Cohen et al., 1991; Herdman et al., 2022; Baranova et al., 2012; Bharat et al., 2017; von Kügelgen et al., 2020; Lupas et al., 1994; Herrmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the bacterium C. crescentus, Ca2+ ions are essential for intra- and inter-molecular stability of the S-layer lattice.
source: In the bacterium C. crescentus, whose S-layer has been investigated in detail, Ca2+ ions are essential for intra- and inter-molecular stability of the S-layer lattice (Herdman et al., 2022; Bharat et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Herdman et al., 2022 and Bharat et al., 2017.

claim: The SLP of the archaeon H. volcanii has been confirmed to bind cations.
source: The SLP of the archaeon H. volcanii has also been recently confirmed to bind cations (von Kügelgen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to von Kügelgen et al., 2021.

claim: The S. acidocaldarius S-layer assembly is a Ca2+-dependent process.
source: The S. acidocaldarius S-layer is no exception and its assembly is a Ca2+-dependent process (Gambelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gambelli et al., 2019.

claim: The SlaA30–1069 cryoEM map did not reveal any anomalous densities that could be attributed to ions.
source: Interestingly, the SlaA30–1069 cryoEM map did not reveal any anomalous densities that could be attributed to ions.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryoEM data.

claim: Cations may be harboured in the D5 and D6 domains of SlaA that were not resolved, and/or at the protein–protein interfaces within the assembled lattice.
source: It is therefore possible that cations are harboured in the D5 and D6 domains that were not resolved, and/or at the protein–protein interfaces within the assembled lattice, which at this point cannot be defined at the side-chain level due to the limited resolution of our subtomogram average.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the absence of ion densities in the cryoEM map.

claim: The H. volcanii and S. acidocaldarius S-layers are currently the only two archaeal S-layers for which complete atomic models are available.
source: Therefore, the H. volcanii and S. acidocaldarius S-layers are currently the only two archaeal S-layers for which complete atomic models are available.
evidence: This is stated based on the current state of knowledge.

claim: H. volcanii is a halophilic archaeon of the Euryarchaeota phylum.
source: H. volcanii is a halophilic archaeon of the Euryarchaeota phylum.
evidence: This is a statement of fact about the organism.

claim: The H. volcanii S-layer is constituted by a single glycosylated SLP named csg.
source: The H. volcanii lattice also exhibits a hexagonal symmetry, but different architecture. The H. volcanii S-layer is constituted by a single glycosylated SLP named csg.
evidence: This is stated based on the structure of H. volcanii S-layer.

claim: SlaA (1424 residues) and csg (827 residues) both consist of six domains.
source: SlaA (1424 residues) and csg (827 residues) both consist of six domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: All csg domains adopt Ig-like folds, whereas SlaA is built up from domains of more complex topology.
source: However, while all csg domains adopt Ig-like folds, SlaA is built up from domains of more complex topology.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of the two structures.

claim: In csg, the domains are arranged linearly, whereas SlaA adopts an extended Y-shape.
source: In csg, the domains are arranged linearly, whereas SlaA adopts an extended Y-shape (Figure 5—figure supplement 4a, b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Ig-like domains are widespread among SLPs in different archaeal phyla, including the order Sulfolobales.
source: Ig-like domains are widespread among SLPs in different archaeal phyla, including the order Sulfolobales (von Kügelgen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to von Kügelgen et al., 2021.

claim: The SlaA protein of Metallosphaera sedula is predicted to consist of seven Ig-like domains.
source: In fact, the SlaA protein of Metallosphaera sedula is predicted to consist of seven Ig-like domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 4d; von Kügelgen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to von Kügelgen et al., 2021 and a figure.

claim: Assembled csg forms hexagonal (13 Å), pentameric (6 Å), and trimeric (10 Å) pores much smaller than the hexagonal (48 Å) and trimeric (85 Å) pores of the S. acidocaldarius lattice.
source: Assembled csg forms hexagonal (13 Å), pentameric (6 Å), and trimeric (10 Å) pores much smaller than the hexagonal (48 Å) and trimeric (85 Å) pores of the S. acidocaldarius lattice.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of the two structures.

claim: In both H. volcanii and S. acidocaldarius S-layers, the pore size is further reduced by glycans projecting into the pores.
source: In both cases, the pore size is further reduced by glycans projecting into the pores.
evidence: This is stated based on the structures of both S-layers.

claim: The glycans could regulate the permeability of the S-layer in a fashion similar to the hydrogel regulating the permeability of the nuclear pore complexes.
source: The glycans could regulate the permeability of the S-layer in a fashion similar to the hydrogel regulating the permeability of the nuclear pore complexes (D'Angelo and Hetzer, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to D'Angelo and Hetzer, 2008.

claim: S. acidocaldarius produces four protein filaments: archaella, A-pili, and UV-inducible pili and threads.
source: S. acidocaldarius produces four such filaments – archaella (Szabó et al., 2007), A-pili (Henche et al., 2012), and UV-inducible pili and threads (Fröls et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Szabó et al., 2007, Henche et al., 2012, and Fröls et al., 2008.

claim: Of the four filaments produced by S. acidocaldarius, only threads, with a diameter of ~40 Å, would be able to pass through the hexagonal pores of the S-layer without the need for a widening of the pores or a partial S-layer disassembly.
source: Of these four filaments, only threads, with a diameter of ~40 Å, would be able to pass through the hexagonal pores of the S-layer without the need for a widening of the pores or a partial S-layer disassembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pore size and filament diameter.

claim: It is speculated that the hexagonal S-layer pores have evolved to accommodate threads, perhaps as a scaffold for their assembly.
source: It is thus tantalising to speculate that the hexagonal S-layer pores have evolved to accommodate threads, perhaps as a scaffold for their assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the pore size and filament diameter.

claim: In H. volcanii, csg assembles around hexameric as well as pentameric pores on the surface of both exosomes and whole cells.
source: In the case of H. volcanii, csg assembles around hexameric as well as pentameric pores on the surface of both exosomes and whole cells (von Kügelgen et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to von Kügelgen et al., 2021.

claim: Pentameric 'defects' in the H. volcanii S-layer confer enough flexibility to the array to encase the cell in areas of low and high membrane curvature.
source: Such pentameric 'defects' confer enough flexibility to the array to encase the cell in areas of low and high membrane curvature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of H. volcanii S-layer.

claim: An analogous phenomenon to pentameric defects was not observed for the S. acidocaldarius S-layer on whole cells or exosomes.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe an analogous phenomenon for the S. acidocaldarius S-layer on whole cells or exosomes.
evidence: This is stated based on the observations of the S. acidocaldarius S-layer.

claim: Symmetry breaks have been observed on S-layers isolated from whole cells at the edges where the lattice changes orientation.
source: However, symmetry breaks have been observed on S-layers isolated from whole cells at the edges where the lattice changes orientation (Pum et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pum et al., 1991.

claim: Additional flexibility in the S. acidocaldarius S-layer may be provided by the SlaA dimeric interface, as well as by loop regions linking the SlaA domains.
source: Furthermore, additional flexibility may be provided by the SlaA dimeric interface, as well as by loop regions linking the SlaA domains.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structure.

claim: Only single loops link D1–D2, D3–D4, D4–D5, and D5–D6 in SlaA.
source: In fact, only single loops link D1–D2, D3–D4, D4–D5, and D5–D6.
evidence: This is stated based on the structure of SlaA.

claim: The reciprocal position of D3–D4 in SlaA is stabilised by the disulphide bond (Cys677–Cys1017).
source: While the reciprocal position of D3–D4 is stabilised by the disulphide bond (Cys677–Cys1017), the loops connecting D1–D2, D4–D5, and D5–D6 may allow the flexibility necessary for SlaA to be incorporated in this highly interwoven, yet malleable protein network.
evidence: This is stated based on the structure of SlaA.

claim: The loops connecting D1–D2, D4–D5, and D5–D6 in SlaA may allow the flexibility necessary for SlaA to be incorporated in the highly interwoven, yet malleable protein network.
source: While the reciprocal position of D3–D4 is stabilised by the disulphide bond (Cys677–Cys1017), the loops connecting D1–D2, D4–D5, and D5–D6 may allow the flexibility necessary for SlaA to be incorporated in this highly interwoven, yet malleable protein network.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structure.

claim: It is proposed that it is likely not pH-induced unfolding or conformational changes in SlaA that cause S-layer disassembly at alkaline pH.
source: Remarkably, SlaA30–1069 proved stable over a vast pH range and its tertiary structure remains virtually unchanged (Figure 3). Thus, we propose that is likely not pH-induced unfolding or conformational changes in SlaA that cause S-layer disassembly at alkaline pH.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the observed structural stability.

claim: The observed reversal in electrostatic potential at rising pH values is a manifestation of deprotonation of amino acid residues, as the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) in the solution decreases.
source: The observed reversal in electrostatic potential at rising pH values is a manifestation of deprotonation of amino acid residues, as the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) in the solution decreases.
evidence: This is an explanation based on chemical principles.

claim: The loss of protons can reduce or abolish the ability of side chains to form hydrogen bonds, and as a result, hydrogen bonds involving these groups can be weakened or broken.
source: The loss of protons can reduce or abolish the ability of side chains to form hydrogen bonds, and as a result, hydrogen bonds involving these groups can be weakened or broken.
evidence: This is an explanation based on chemical principles.

claim: The weakening or abolishment of hydrogen bonds (in particular those involving acidic amino acids) could be a key factor in pH-induced disassembly.
source: The weakening or abolishment of these bonds (in particular those involving acidic amino acids) could therefore be a key factor in pH-induced disassembly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on chemical principles.

claim: The lowering of the pH will re-protonate acidic residues, facilitate the formation of hydrogen bonds, and thus the assembly of the S-layer.
source: Conversely, the lowering of the pH will re-protonate these residues, facilitate the formation of hydrogen bonds, and thus the assembly of the S-layer.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on chemical principles.

claim: pH stability predictions suggest virtually no difference in pH-dependent protein stability across ionic strength and pH values for both SlaA30–1069 and the full length SlaA protein.
source: Considerations regarding the pH stability of SlaA30–1069 can be extended to the entirety of the protein using pH stability predictions, which suggest virtually no difference in pH-dependent protein stability across ionic strength and pH values for both SlaA30–1069 and the full length SlaA protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 5a–d).
evidence: This is stated based on pH stability predictions and supported by figures.

claim: Domains D5 and D6 of SlaA equally do not unfold at alkaline pH.
source: This suggests that domains D5 and D6 equally do not unfold at alkaline pH.
evidence: This is an inference based on pH stability predictions.

claim: Analogous predictions of protein stability were obtained for SlaB, where the net charge is slightly positive across pH 2–8.
source: Analogous predictions of protein stability were obtained for SlaB (Figure 5—figure supplement 5e, f), where the net charge is slightly positive across pH 2–8.
evidence: This is stated based on pH stability predictions and supported by figures.

claim: Among SlaA, SlaB, RsaA, and csg, SlaA and SlaB are expected to be the most stable at different pH values.
source: Among SlaA, SlaB, RsaA, and csg, we observe that SlaA and SlaB are expected to be the most stable at different pH values.
evidence: This is stated based on pH stability predictions.

claim: Csg is most stable at acidic pH and progressively less so at neutral and alkaline pH.
source: Notably, csg is most stable at acidic pH and progressively less so at neutral and alkaline pH. This prediction is confirmed by experimental data (Rodrigues-Oliveira et al., 2019), which additionally showed pH-dependent protein folding rearrangements and protein unfolding.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rodrigues-Oliveira et al., 2019.

claim: The pH stability prediction does not include glycosylation.
source: It is to be considered that this prediction does not include glycosylation (Hebditch and Warwicker, 2019), which enhances S-layer stability, especially in the case of Sulfolobales (Jarrell et al., 2014; Meyer and Albers, 2014; Meyer et al., 2011; Yurist-Doutsch et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Glycosylation enhances S-layer stability, especially in the case of Sulfolobales.
source: It is to be considered that this prediction does not include glycosylation (Hebditch and Warwicker, 2019), which enhances S-layer stability, especially in the case of Sulfolobales (Jarrell et al., 2014; Meyer and Albers, 2014; Meyer et al., 2011; Yurist-Doutsch et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jarrell et al., 2014, Meyer and Albers, 2014, Meyer et al., 2011, and Yurist-Doutsch et al., 2008.

claim: The resilience of SlaA at temperature and pH shifts can likely be attributed to the high glycosylation level and the fact that ~56% of SlaA30–1069 has a defined secondary structure.
source: The resilience of SlaA at temperature and pH shifts can likely be attributed to two main factors: the high glycosylation level, and the fact that ~56% of SlaA30–1069 has a defined secondary structure, which allows the formation of intramolecular bonds (Vogt et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Vogt et al., 1997.

claim: ~56% of SlaA30–1069 has a defined secondary structure, which allows the formation of intramolecular bonds.
source: The resilience of SlaA at temperature and pH shifts can likely be attributed to two main factors: the high glycosylation level, and the fact that ~56% of SlaA30–1069 has a defined secondary structure, which allows the formation of intramolecular bonds (Vogt et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated based on the structure and supported by a citation to Vogt et al., 1997.

claim: S-layers are often necessary for the survival of microorganisms in nature but can also be of great interest for synthetic biology.
source: S-layers are often necessary for the survival of microorganisms in nature but can also be of great interest for synthetic biology.
evidence: This is a general statement about S-layers.

claim: A greater understanding of S-layer structural details will strongly aid their nanotechnological uses, which have already shown remarkable potential in biomedical and environmental applications.
source: Therefore, a greater understanding of their structural details will strongly aid their nanotechnological uses, which have already shown remarkable potential in biomedical (Lanzoni-Mangutchi et al., 2022; Luo et al., 2019; Fioravanti et al., 2022) and environmental applications (Charrier et al., 2019; Pallares et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2021; Schuster and Sleytr, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.
